title: China Air Freight Rates Hold Amid Winter Capacity Shift
metaDescription: Air cargo rates stabilise at $3.13/kg as airlines add winter freighter links to Asia, Europe, and the Americas to offset Golden Week dips.
bottomLine: Global air cargo rates held steady at $3.13 per kilo in early October despite a volume dip from China's Golden Week. Airlines are now adding winter freighter capacity to Asia, Europe, and the Americas to shuffle capacity for Q4.

stories.headline: Global air cargo rates hold at $3.13 per kilo
stories.tldr: Average global air cargo rates remained stable at $3.13 per kilo in the first two weeks of October 2026.
stories.whatHappened:
WorldACD Global Data reports that full market rates, combining spot and contract, held steady at $3.13 per kilo. Global tonnage rose 9% year on year in week 41, which ran from 5 to 11 October.

Spot rates from Asia Pacific origins fell 3% week on week to $4.83 per kilo. Tonnages from the region declined for a third consecutive week, a trend attributed to China's Golden Week holiday.

Other regional spot rates also dipped. Middle East and South Asia origins fell 2% week on week. Africa offset these declines with a 10% rise in spot rates.
stories.whyItMatters:
If you are shipping high-value electronics or fashion from Shenzhen or Ningbo, the Golden Week dip has given you a brief window of stability. The $4.83 spot rate for Asia Pacific is a slight reprieve, but do not mistake it for a trend.

Jet fuel prices and surcharges are still pushing your total cost up. If you rely on spot rates for your Q4 peak, you are exposed to the volatility seen in the Africa lanes. You should lock in contract rates now before the November rush.

For those of you moving goods into the US or EU, the year on year tonnage growth of 9% means the planes are still full. You will not see a collapse in pricing even if weekly volumes flicker.
stories.hotTake: The Golden Week dip is a fake-out. Every operator knows that the volume doesn't vanish, it just shifts by ten days. I expect spot rates to spike again by early November as the backlog clears and the December deadline hits.
actions: Lock in contract rates for November shipments to avoid spot volatility
Audit your fuel surcharge line items to see how much jet fuel costs are eating your margin

stories.headline: Airlines add winter freighter links to Asia and Americas
stories.tldr: Airlines are increasing freighter capacity between Asia, Europe, and the Americas to support winter tech exports and manufacturing hubs.
stories.whatHappened:
Air Canada Cargo launched new 767-30F services connecting to Amsterdam, Monterrey, and Panama City. Lufthansa Cargo increased frequencies to the US, while Air France added a new link to Cairo.

JAL and Cathay Cargo added more transpacific options. These moves come as freight forwarders renegotiate contracts for the winter season to manage the capacity shuffle between the major distribution hubs.
stories.whyItMatters:
The addition of links to Monterrey and Panama City is a signal. If you are sourcing from China but diversifying assembly into Mexico or Central America, your air bridge just got stronger.

More transpacific options from JAL and Cathay Cargo mean you have more leverage when negotiating with your forwarder. You are no longer beholden to a single carrier's schedule for your urgent Q4 refills.

For those shipping into Europe, the Air Canada Amsterdam link provides an alternative routing that might bypass some of the congestion at primary hubs during the peak season rush.
stories.hotTake: Carriers are chasing the 'China Plus One' shift in real time. They are adding capacity to Latin American hubs because that is where the new factories are. If you haven't looked at Mexico as a transit point, you are missing the shift.
actions: Ask your forwarder for quotes on the new Air Canada Monterrey and Panama City routes
Compare transpacific rates between Cathay and JAL for your November shipments

stories.headline: Chinese EV makers move production to Europe to avoid tariffs
stories.tldr: Chinese car manufacturers plan to build factories in Europe or use idle plants to sidestep EU import quotas and tariffs.
stories.whatHappened:
Chinese carmakers are facing an EU import quota on hybrid electric vehicles. To maintain sales growth, they are planning to invest billions of yuan in local European production.

Companies are looking at two paths: building their own new factories or leasing idle plants from existing international brands to maintain their go-global drive in one of the world's major automotive markets.
stories.whyItMatters:
This is a blueprint for any high-value ecommerce seller facing aggressive EU tariffs. When the cost of importing exceeds the cost of local assembly, you move the final stage of production.

If you sell bulky goods or electronics with high tariff profiles, you need to analyse if a European 'finishing' centre or assembly hub makes sense. It removes the quota risk and cuts the final mile delivery time.

This move also signals that Chinese manufacturers are committed to the European market for the long term. They are not just exporting; they are embedding their operations to survive the trade war.
stories.hotTake: The era of shipping finished goods from China to the EU is ending for high-tariff categories. I expect more 'semi-knocked-down' kits shipping from China to be finished in Poland or Hungary.
actions: Review your EU import quotas and tariff costs for 2027
Research third-party assembly partners in Eastern Europe to reduce landed costs

stories.headline: US East and Gulf coast ports expand for non-China trade
stories.tldr: US East and Gulf coast ports are launching projects to accommodate larger ships and expanding trade outside of China.
stories.whatHappened:
Multiple projects have been planned, started, or are nearing completion this year. These gateways, both large and small, are preparing their infrastructure for larger vessels.

The goal of these investments is to support expanding trade volumes that originate from regions outside of China as the US diversifies its supply chain imports.
stories.whyItMatters:
If you are shifting your sourcing to Southeast Asia or Latin America, your entry points into the US are getting a capacity boost. This reduces the reliance on the congested West Coast ports.

Better infrastructure on the East and Gulf coasts means you can potentially lower your drayage costs and reduce dwell times for goods coming from non-Chinese origins.

For those still sourcing from China, this is a signal that the US is actively building the infrastructure to make it easier for you to move your production elsewhere. The physical capacity is catching up to the policy goals.
stories.hotTake: The US is literally building the exit ramp for China sourcing. These port expansions aren't just about 'growth', they are about decoupling the physical flow of goods from the Chinese mainland.
actions: Analyse the transit times for your non-China shipments via Gulf coast ports
Compare East Coast vs West Coast drayage costs for your 2027 planning

faq.question: What are the current air freight rates from China?
faq.answer: Average global full-market air cargo rates are stable at $3.13 per kilo. Spot rates from Asia Pacific origins have dipped to $4.83 per kilo following the Golden Week holiday.

faq.question: Are there new air freight routes to the Americas from Asia?
faq.answer: Yes. Air Canada Cargo has introduced new 767-30F services to Monterrey and Panama City. JAL and Cathay Cargo have also increased transpacific options.

faq.question: How are Chinese companies avoiding EU import tariffs?
faq.answer: Chinese manufacturers are shifting to local production within Europe by building new factories or leasing idle plants to sidestep import quotas and tariffs.

faq.question: What is happening with US port infrastructure?
faq.answer: US East and Gulf coast ports are launching projects to handle larger ships and increase capacity for trade originating from countries other than China.
